title: Keep a moving head's camera on a moving figure, and stop at the lamp
instruction: Hold the bar of the moving head and turn it so that the camera stays on the figure as it moves along its rail. When the red lamp comes on, press the stop button within 1 s while keeping the camera on the figure. When the figure has stopped, let go of the bar.
context: Camera Operators (O*NET 27-4031) keep a moving subject in frame by panning a camera on a moving head with its long bar, and stop on a cue without losing the shot. The subject's moves and stops change by seed, so no planned path fits, and the aim must follow what the subject does.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a table; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm, heights above the table. A camera on a video pan head stands at (34, 0): a black foot 14 cm across and 1.2 thick, an aluminium column 4 cm across, and a pan deck 7 cm across, pan axis 10 up. On the deck, a black camera body, 14 x 6 x 7 cm, with a lens 4.8 cm across and 6 long, 20 cm long in all, points +x at the start; behind it, a steel pan bar 1.8 cm across and 30 long, 12.5 up, with a rubber grip 2.8 cm across and 10 long centred 22 cm behind the axis. A bright yellow line runs along the bar and the camera. The moving part weighs 0.4 kg and pans 36 degrees each way. Its fluid drag is 0.6 N m per rad/s, so panning at 30 degrees per second takes about 1.4 N at the grip, plus 0.05 N m of friction, about 0.2 N there. In a real trial, a phone films the camera's screen, which has a central band marked on it 6 degrees wide, together with the lamp and button. A plastic figure of a small person, 17 cm tall, in a blue shirt with arms, a face and hair, stands on a 5 x 5 cm carriage on a motor-driven belt rail at x 84, 50 cm ahead of the head: an aluminium rail 68 cm long, 6 wide and 2 high, with a black rubber belt, carrying the figure from y -30 to 30, starting at y 0. A red LED lamp, a globe 6 cm across, stands on a grey post at (68, 38), 14 up, dark at the start. A red stop button, 5.6 cm across and 1.5 tall, stands on a grey steel block, 9 x 9 x 5 cm, at (30, 45), its top 6.5 up, out of the right arm's reach; it travels 8 mm against a 300 N/m spring and registers at 5 mm, at about 1.5 N. From 5 s the belt plays a schedule set by the seed: moves at 8 to 15 cm/s to random places, with stops of 0.8 to 2.2 s, for about 30 s. The lamp comes on just after a move starts.
scoring: Timed with a stopwatch on a phone film of the camera's screen, lamp and button; a tape for the fingers. Count the seconds from the belt's start to the lamp with the figure's centre outside the screen's central band, 3 degrees each side. 1.0 when that is at most 6 s, the button is pressed within 1 s after the lamp with the figure in the band, and at the end fingers are at least 3 cm from bar and button for 1 s. 0.75 when it is at most 6 s, but the press or the fingers fail. 0.5 when it is at most 12 s. 0 otherwise. A press before the lamp stops the recording: all the time from there to the lamp counts as outside.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Bring the bar and figure back to the middle. In a real trial, a stepper driver plays a table of times for the seed, and an output lights the lamp.
fidelity: Rigid-body physics at 240 Hz on GPU. The aim is the head's angle, with no screen rendered: a real trial reads it from the camera's own screen. The belt is a stiff drive on a joint, following the schedule. The bar has no weight. One arm can track; both arms are needed only for the press credit, as an arm that leaves the bar loses the aim.
